blocks.x: I'll make a note that we're recording an interview with Mr. Narvin Kimball out at 3537 Calhoun, and the date is November, let me think, what it is, is it 24th?
25th.

25th already, 1961. And this is Bill Russell. Do you mind giving your full name? Narvin Henry Kimball. I noticed in the old times, a lot of times people would call you Henry Kimball Jr., and your father, was his name also Narvin?
No, his name was Henry. Just Henry. And they would call me Henry because of my father. They would call me Little Henry, or they would call me Henry Kimball Jr.
So for a long time I didn't even know your name was Narvin, your first name.
Yes.
Because everyone has called you Henry. Do you mind telling us when you were born and where, what part of the city and so on?
I was born on March 2, 1909. And we... Right here in New Orleans? In New Orleans, yes. In the area of the Irish Channel.
Oh, yes.
Around 7th, between St. Thomas and Chippewa.
Oh, yes. I know about where that is. I know St. Thomas and 7th. It was down between the river and Magazine, is that right? That's right. It really was the Irish Channel then, wasn't it?
Yeah, definitely.

Do you remember anything about your childhood? Did you live there long with... I've heard a lot of tales about how it was sort of a tough section of the Irish people down there and all. Well... Did you remember much of those times?

I can remember quite a bit of it. During that time there was quite an association between the Irish and the Negroes who lived in the area. The parents would have their children to remain if they went in town to do shopping. They would have their children to remain with either. If one of the Irish people had to go, they would ask my mother to keep their children and my mother would do the same by them. Now, during those times particularly, the boys didn't appreciate other boys visiting from other neighborhoods. If someone came from the 10th Ward into the 11th Ward, the whites and colors would fight together. And if they came in from either ward, they would always fight. Even if we would attempt to visit and other was, we too would have to fight.
That's strange isn't it?
Now, they would get angry with us many times if we wouldn't fight with them and would fight us. But it was all over again. We would play sandlot ball and it would be completed as such.
Do you remember many early bands or parades down in that section?

Well, during that time I was quite a youngster but I always had an appreciation for my family. I always had an appreciation for music. They would have wagons. The advertising would be on most weekends, lawn parties would be given in the area. That would be in backyards, you know. I've been to a couple myself in late years. Yes. And to give the proper advertisement for such, they would have the bands that go around on the street. And they would have the tromboats and play. And what intrigued me more than anything else during that time was to see the trombone on the back. I suppose that's where the tailgate trombone came from. To see the trombone, they would be sliding back and forth on the horn. Did they put the bass back there too? The bass violin and the trombone were on the very back, very end. And if sometimes they would have two bands, they would meet, and they would back the two wagons right to each other and stand there for half an hour or so and they would play against each other. There was a natural appreciation for just playing. Men would just love to play.

I wonder, if I'm going to interrupt you, I was going to ask more about your father, if you can tell us even some of the things about his life. That is, if you know just when he was born and when he died, we don't have that information exactly. We might, I haven't seen his birth date, we might be able to check when he died. But if you can remember approximately the day of the year, if you don't remember the exact birthday or anything.
My father would be 85 years old if he were living now. 85 now.
Yes.
And he was born on March the 24th, the same month. And I was born on the 24th of March.
So that would be...
This is 61...
86, 1886 would that be? Hmm.
Oh no, more than that. 81.
Seventh or in it. If you were born in 81 he'd be 80 years old. So he'd be 76. So he'd be 76. 1876 about. Approximately. About that time. I don't remember the exact date. Yes.
Did he ever play anything besides string bass?
Yes, he played the string bass. Did you? Yes, he played the sousaphone. Did he play in parades too or just an artist?
I don't remember his having played in parades because he always played the bass violin until the later years, about maybe 10 or 15 years before he died.
Oh, and by the way, just remember the year he died then?
It was in 32 or 33. 32 or 33. He was about 53 years old when he died. He wasn't old at all then.
No, he wasn't. We wouldn't consider that even hardly middle age. Some people say he's still young.
Yes.
One kind of thing a long time ago when we think of him as being one of the pioneers, one of the old men in jazz, but he wasn't old at all.
No, he wasn't an old man. No. When I was a child, I could remember his playing with John Robichaux's orchestra. Oh, yes.
I was going to ask. I knew that he'd heard he played with them and I've had pictures of him playing on the boat with Fate Marable.
Well, that was in later years. Yes.
But, uh... Did he ever say if he ever started on any other instrument like guitar or...
No, I remember his saying that he was taught by Professor Nicholson. Oh, yeah. Nicholson or Nicholson. I think it's Nicholson. Nicholson. Nicholson.

There was a whole family of those. I know Professor Minetta talks about him. Yes. He studied. And, uh, Jellero Martin, the Ferdinand Martin studied with one of the, uh, Nicholson's too. They had a school. I've seen the ads of their school. They ran the little music school. Yeah.
His, uh, the only instrument that I knew of his playing was the bass violin and then in later years he played the sousaphone.
Did he ever say how old he was when he started? I guess not too young if he just started on the bass.

Well, yes, he did remember. I do remember his, his mentioning about, uh, where Xavier Prep is now, it was called Southern University then. Mm-hmm. And, uh, he started in a school band there when he was, uh, uh, when he was a boy in school. He started playing in a school band. He did play another instrument. He started on a small violin. Oh, here it is. That's right. I thought maybe he might have done something like that.
He did, yes.

It came to me. Uh, he started on a small violin. And, um, the bass is a pretty big instrument to start out on. Yes. Then he, he later, uh, started on the string bass. And he remained with the bass violin for quite some years. In fact, he played the bass violin until he died. Um.
That's the school, it was on St. Charles Southern? I don't know the location.
I mean where Xavier is. No, uh, out at Sonya magazine. Oh, on magazine.
Oh, sure.
Yes, that was, that was called Southern University. Southern University. Oh, I had Southern University. Both my mother and he attended that school. Yes.
But there's another school, uh, called New Orleans University was on St. Charles.
Well, that's the one that I attended.

Oh, and Bunk Johnson went to Pops Foster, told me he went there, you know, George Foster, the bass player. Yes. And Emmanuel Moneta did too. He went there when he was a boy. Not long, but maybe a year or so.
Well, uh, my first school was at James Lewis School, uh, in the elementary grades, and then I finished from McDonough 35 High School and, uh, New Orleans University later. Uh.

Anything else about your father or any, it doesn't have to be in special order, if you can remember, or anything else, that he might have told you about how he started music like with Robichaux, was that his first band, do you think? He must have probably played something else too.

No, that wasn't the first band. Um, he played, uh, around here locally with, uh, some of the older musicians. Uh, I can't remember just who they were, but I can remember this, that in the first organized, in a recognized organized group that he played was Robichaux's band.
Robichaux's band.

Because, uh, he was, uh, quite young when he started playing with them. Now, he had played previously with others. Uh, but, uh, when I was about eight or nine years old, uh, he took me down to the Lyric Theater. They were playing down there. The orchestra played in the pit. Yes, I knew that Robichaux had that.
And your father was playing bass with him.

He was playing bass violin. Charlie McCurdys was, McCurdys was playing, uh, clarinet. Mr. Vic Gaspert was playing trombone. Uh, Mr. Walter Brundy was playing drums. Andrew Kimball was playing, uh, trumpet.
Well, I think I would, uh, I've heard that he was no relation to your family. Is that true, or, uh?
He was. He was? Yes, that was my father's brother.
Oh, I didn't know. Oh, I heard he was no relation. Somebody told me he was no relation. I didn't know. Uh.

So, I should have known. I didn't know that they were related until after I had started to play music. And I met Andrew Kimball and Mrs. Margaret Kimball in Shreveport. And Bill Matthews, the trombone player, came to me and told me that he wanted to, that Mr. Kimball wanted to talk with me. And I went over and he asked me about, did I know my father's father? And I told him, yes, I know him. And he asked what was his name. I said his name was Henry Kimball also. That's your grandfather's name. Yes. And, uh, he asked whether or not, uh, I might be mistaken because, uh, they were four brothers. It was Ed, Benny, Henry, and James.
Did the other brothers play any instruments?
No. No. No. They, that group of brothers had a quartet.
They sang. They did sing them. Yeah. By the way, did your grandfather, Henry Kimball, play any instruments? No. He didn't play anything. Or sing or instruments?
He sang. He sang. No.
No one else.

My sister, one of my sisters attempted to learn the piano when she was in high school. And, uh, she completed one or two grades, but she didn't follow it through. And then I started on the piano. When was your first instrument? That was my first instrument. About how old were you?
About seven or eight years old.

That's right. And, uh, I didn't like the piano. I didn't like that because at that time, uh, they had things that was called your music role. Oh yeah. It'd fold up. And sometimes it was made out of plush and different colors like that. And they passed down from my sister to me her music role that she had to take her music book in. And, uh, the fellas would kid me and call me a sister. I didn't like that. So I just continued playing, uh, the violin. So many girls played piano.
That's what I heard too. That a lot of boys, they thought it would be all sisters.

Yeah, and the violin. Uh, that's the first instrument that my father wanted me to learn. My mother wanted me to learn the violin. But, uh, I didn't like the violin. The first instrument that I had, I made, it was out of a seagull box.
Sort of a banjo type?

It was made out of a seagull box and in the manual training room at school I made a neck and made the pegs to put in it. And, uh, a friend of my father's name, Mr. Coochie Martin, he was a guitar player. Oh yeah.
So he was one of the family of the Martins?

One was a drummer and the other one was the... That was the Henry Martin that was a drummer. That's right. Well, the one that they called Coochie Martin. Whenever he would break one of his guitar strings my dad would bring it home to me.
Oh yeah.

And, uh, use it on a little shirt. And I would, uh, tune it up and, uh, not with the proper tuning, I would just tune it up to my imagination, what sounded like a chord to me. Yeah. And would strum without the finger, just move my fingers from one place to another across the bar, you know. And, uh, I sang, in fact my sisters and I sang, we sing nicely together. Uh, we had what was called a kitchen trio in the afternoons when the dishes were being washed we used to sing. Uh, uh, my father would appreciate our singing and told us that we sang very well. Uh, getting back to the instrument.

Oh, one other question, too, while I think of it, uh, Coochie Martin, which band was your father playing in at that time? Do you remember, was that, did Coochie Martin play with Robichoke too? I don't remember much about it. No.
They're all dead, I guess, in the Martin family. There was a band that was named Onfrey and Duran.
Oh, Maurice Duran?
Maurice Duran, a trumpet player.
By the way, I heard just yesterday or the day before that he died in California. Is that right?
Uh-huh.

He had been here a year or so ago, his father had been sick, still living down in the ninth ward, uh, the Zardy Street. I met him in California, and I met him here years ago. So, uh, I guess it must be true, two different people told me they heard from California these guys.
It most likely is.
A couple days ago.
It was, uh, called Onfrey and Duran, Willie Onfrey, the clarinet player.
The old man, not, not the Willie. No, no.
The Willie, he was the youngster then.
He, the, the...
Yeah, the clarinet player.
Yeah, the one that played.
And, uh, Duran, and Johnny St. Cyr, and, uh, Coochie Martin. No, not Coochie Martin, he wasn't in that group. I don't remember what group.
But your father worked with them then? Yes, he worked with them. And, uh, and, uh, well, you, uh, I interrupted you were going to tell about your first instrument and all your guitar and the band.

Well, I made that, I made that, uh, supposedly ukulele or banjo, whatever it was, and cut a hole in it, and would play with that. And, uh, I was in high school. And, uh, when I was in high school, later on when I went to high school, I, uh, I bought a ukulele. I had a little job in the afternoons after school. And, uh, I saved my money until I had about seven dollars and I bought a ukulele. Uh-huh. And brought it home on a Friday evening. Uh, Red Allen and I went to school. He was my upperclassman, though. And, uh, where were you living? Was he going to school over this side of the river? I thought he'd maybe be over an hour there.

No, he was at McDonald's 35 then. He was the only in high school. Yeah. And, uh, he played the ukulele very well. And, uh, I liked the way he played it. And, uh, it developed quite a bit of popularity for him being a ukulele player.

And, uh, I wanted to play the ukulele also. So, I bought one on a Friday evening and I was, uh, I was, uh, I was, uh, I was, uh, a little boy. And so, I bought one on a Friday evening and bought a chord chart. And that Monday morning when I came back I could play a little too. Yeah, yeah. And, uh, I continued to play that. And, uh, I began to develop some popularity as well as a ukulele player. And, uh, my father, this is the beginning of when he was playing on the steam of Capitol then. It was the same as the steam of Sydney before the Capitol was here. And he played on that. And, um, that was around the time that, uh, he had started playing there around 1918 and 1919. But I didn't start in high school until 1922. You see, I'm trying to associate the time with that. You would have been about the sixth or seventh grade then maybe when, um, when you started
on the boat.
Yes. When, uh, did you get to hear that band ever?

I, and, you get on the boat or hear it from over on the wharf and they'd play before they'd start? How did it sound? Yes. They made a record once. I don't believe your father's on it. I think the Pop Swaster played the bass at that time. And the record was, it wasn't electric recording. It's not too good a record. It's hard to tell from that whether, how wonderful the band is. But everybody talks about how great it was. That's when they had Armstrong and the St. Cyr.
Well, my daddy was there when Armstrong came on the boat.
Yes. He's on that picture with them and St. Cyr, I forget who else was in the band.
And, um, at that time my daddy and Louis were roommates. They lived in the Texas above the boat when they traveled from here to St. Paul. And, um, they became quite friendly.
Well, Baby Dodds was in the band too. Baby Dodds, that's right.

I knew Baby Dodds, that's right. Baby Dodds, he was in the band. I remember, I remember seeing that picture. Um, they had a violinist on that boat too. He was in the band. He played violin and mellophone. I can't think of his name.
You said, David, remember, did it David Jones that played mellophone? David Jones played out there.
He played out there also.
He played sax too. And, uh, trying to think, did he play violin? I don't think so.
He played, one of the person that I was speaking about played mellophone also. Because on the picture I can remember the mellophone being there.
Yeah, I remember.
Well, before I had completed high school, my daddy bought me a banjo. Regular four string.
Ten of banjo.
Ten of banjo.
Ten of banjo.
And I was being taught by Willie Foster, that's Pop Foster's brother. Oh yeah, I interviewed him up in Baton Rouge.
You did. About two years ago.
Yes, he taught me.
She was still living. She was 106 years old then. Yes. That's right. But had a stroke, so she couldn't talk.

And, uh, he taught me the banjo. For about a year and a half I was instructed by him. And he left to go to California. During that time he was playing on the Steamer Capitol. And, uh, through the friendship that existed between my father and fate, uh, I was given an opportunity to play on the Steamer Capitol. And they called me in for a rehearsal. I left them here on a Saturday and on that Sunday evening we had to rehearse in St. Louis on the boat.
Had you finished high school then about that time?

Yes, I had finished high school. I was in my first year of college. And, uh, the dean, Dean Hayes at the university arranged, it was near the final examination time. And he arranged, it was about three weeks prior to that time, and he arranged that I would take my examinations. And, uh, if I passed the examinations, it was decided between my mother, my parents, and he that if I passed that I would go. And if I didn't pass, well, I would have to remain. So, I went. And, uh, that Sunday evening I never will forget, but it called for rehearsal. And, uh, all of the band was naturally intact because they had been playing their repertoire. And they passed their banjo book to me. Well, I hadn't had any big band experience before. And most of the little bands that I had been, not most of them, but the one band particularly that I had been playing with before I went up there was Paul Mollier. I wanted to mention that in there. Have you heard of him?
I've heard of him. There's nothing about him though, actually.
Well, we'll get back to him.
I've heard of him just the mention.

I played with Paul Mollier's group. And, uh, they passed the book to me and started from the front of the book. It was, uh, during those years they didn't have the cymbals written over the chords that you play as a banjo player. You actually had to read the notes. Read the chords, yeah. And they were playing everything in the natural tempos that they were supposed to be played. And, uh, well, being frightened and being in a new environment, I just became frustrated. I didn't know what to do.
It's a tough thing to read that off its site.
It was.
It was an experienced group.

And, uh, I didn't do so very good at the rehearsal. So the captain of the boat came up and asked, he said, what's the matter? He asked my dad, he said, what's wrong? He said, well he's nervous for one thing and then he's excited too. So he asked me, he said, is there anything that you feel that you can play at lib or you would like to play, to give me a general idea of how you play? So I said, well I can play Tiger Rag. And, uh, I played that. And the band played it in an up tempo. And, uh, I just went away with it. So he was very well pleased with what I had done then. And he said to the group then, he said, that this fellow has, this young fellow has a fine potential. And he expected the assistance from every man in the group in his spare time to help me. Because by the time we had completed the tour, we were going, we were leaving to go to St. Paul and then come back to New Orleans. He said that he expected to have me play many numbers as I had played Tiger Rag. Well it worked out just about that way. And, uh, when I came back to the band. Who else was in the band?
Can you remember almost everybody else?

Yes, I can remember almost all of the fellas there. We had Floyd Campbell, he was playing drums. Faith Marable playing piano. Tom Lovingood playing piano. My father was playing bass, violin, and the sousaphone. Willie Humphrey was playing clarinet and tenor sax. Bert, oh, what's Bert's name?
Who did he play?

He played saxophone, alto saxophone and baritone. And his brother-in-law played alto saxophone and baritone. They had three sax, and Nathaniel Story played trombone. Oh yeah. Dewey Jackson played trumpet. And, any other trumpets? I'm trying to think of other trumpets. First, second trumpet. Oh, Irvin Randolph. Oh yeah. Irvin Randolph. Yeah, I knew him in Chicago, yeah. Yes.
He worked with Louis Armstrong up there. That's right.
Irvin Randolph. He played second trumpet. That was just about the lineup then. I was playing banjo then. And, uh, Floyd Campbell sang beautifully. He had a very nice voice.
And he made some records with Charlie Creff I believe.

Well, Charlie Creff joined the band later. He was in the band. The same band. The same band. Because Dewey Jackson didn't come down with the, he came down for a while but he left to go back to St. Louis. And Charlie Creff came down. And, um, Charlie Creff was friendly with the banjoists that I replaced, Red Brown. I replaced Red Brown.
Was he from St. Louis? He was from that area.
Up in there. And, uh, he was also friendly with, uh, Morgan the bass player.
Was that Al Morgan?
Al Morgan.
Yeah.

I didn't know him. Yeah. And, uh, Charlie Creff was quite a celebrity then. He had done, uh, quite a few recordings. And when he came down, seemingly he was dissatisfied with, uh, uh, my father and me as musicians. And, uh, he influenced fate to the extent that we were given our notice.
He probably won some of his St. Louis friends.

No, he wanted Al Morgan and Red Brown back in the band. Oh, oh. And, uh, it happened just that way. Well, uh, it was, it was, uh, to my advantage that, uh, things did happen that way because the boat was getting ready to go up again and, and it was near around the time the school was closing and I had to remain here for examinations again. And, uh, I had had, uh, a week of illness. I was off for one or two weeks. I was ill. My father had a tooth extracted and the injection that he had had in his lip, temporary paralyzed his lip. And he told the, the, uh, captain on the boat that he would ever be able to play and, uh, a lot of everything.
Yeah.
Now, uh, before I went on the boat I was playing with, uh, Paul Mollier's group. It was a family band. What did he play?
I can't even remember right now.
Paul Mollier played trumpet.
Trumpet, yeah. He had, uh, He's not living, I guess, any place, is he?

No, he isn't living. Uh, most of those men are dead. It's, uh, with the exception of his son. He has a, Lil Paul is still a drummer. I don't know if he's still in New Orleans. I haven't seen or heard of him either. But Ernest Mollier was a clarinet player, his son. And, uh, Paul's uncle was named Paul Mollier. He was the bass violin player. And I played banjo. And, uh,
Are they from downtown?

Yes, they were from on, in the same block where the, um, the Jazz Museum is. Oh, down on Dumaine. On Dumaine Street between St. Claude and Burgundy. He was living on the uptown side in the ten hundred block, about 1022, that's where he was living, right in that area.
Yup.
And we would rehearse down at the house and the people would gather around. There was an old man playing trombone, uh, Mr. Joe Petit, he was a very old man.
Oh sure, I knew him.

He played trombone in that band. He was a, he was a, uh, quite a personable fellow. He, uh, I can always remember, he used to kid me and tell me about my being the youngest one in the group. And that, uh, when we would go out on the road somebody would kidnap me and leave beyond that. We, we traveled one time down to Delco Island to play.
Did he, uh, did Joe Petit play slide or the valve? Slide. I know he started out on the valve, I guess most of the new ones.
Well he had both. Uh, and, uh, it just as he felt, sometimes he would bring the slide and then other times he would bring the valve trombone. But, uh, he was. Some good pictures of him.

And one time, uh, I, I made a record. He, uh, a friend of me, of mine told me that he'd once expressed the wish to make a record. So once when I was recording, uh, Bunk Johnson and, uh, this happened to be Wooden Joe's band. Yeah, he made these with Wooden Joe, Nicholas. Uh huh. And, um, uh, Burbank. And we had him just, he didn't even have his trombone. He'd given up trombone. He used Jim Robinson's trombone. A couple of numbers played Careless Love and St. Louis Blues. He was quite deaf. He had trouble first hearing what key they were in. Yes. He had tried a couple of times and he got onto it. Without any teeth, too. No teeth, but he still doesn't play.

That's right, because when, I can remember that was something else that I remember about him. When he was playing the trombone when, uh, we were with Paul Moyer's group, he had one tooth on the side. It was the, the eye, the eye tooth. And he would place it on the side of the eye tooth and would brace his lip for his embouchure. A strong lip. And he played.
Even when he hadn't played for years, he, after ten minutes time, he'd fill the horn.
He'd fill the horn.
Yeah. Nice tom.

And, um, when I was called to play with the, with the group on the boat, uh, I gave due respect to, uh, Mr. Mollier and told him that, uh, that opportunity was presenting myself. And he said he felt proud of me and that he wanted to see me make it. Because at that time, musicians, they seemingly had, um, they had a mania for playing on the boat. And two, they felt that when you played on the boat that you had been given quite a bit of recognition because we'd always had good bands.
Yeah, he got to travel and see a little bit of the country there too, I guess. Yeah.
And, um, yeah. Then after my playing on there, uh, on the boat, I joined Sidney Desvines group for about three months. Were they working here in town?
I know he was on the boat sometime too.

He was on the boat in later years, but that, at that time, he wasn't on the boat then. Uh, he was playing locally, playing spots from different places. And, uh, I remained with him for about three months. That's the band Pops Foster and Walter Pichon, Louis Bauerrand, that was, and I, we made the rhythm section. And Eddie Cherie and, uh, Adolf Alexandria and Walter Pearson was the saxophone section.

Oh, yes. I know, I met a man on the train, Professor Lynette and I went out there two years ago, and on the way back, he was a cook on the Southern Pacific, if that's the same man. He'd once played with Celestan, he'd said, and he'd best recognize him just walking through the train. So, then he visited him. I met him, that's the first time. I never did the same since.
Yes, he's a light-fledged follower. Yes, he lives in California.
Yes, he does.
That's the man, yeah.
I guess there wasn't any relation to the other Pearson, Eddie Pearson, who played the trombone.
I think that they were related, they were cousins. Cousins, huh? Yes, I think that they were related.
I just asked him, we've got to talk to him in about a half a minute. Just as the train is going over to Huey Long Ridge, he'd happen to be coming in, getting ready to get off.
During that time, they had bands playing out here at the Bulls Club at 8th and Ramport.
Where the Elks are.
At the Elks are where the Elks are.
There were big lawn parties out there too, I guess.

There were big lawns on both sides. Yeah, right. It was a contest every Tuesday night between different groups. And I played with Sidney Desvins band first. And after about three or four months, I joined Celestan's band. And I remained with them for about eight or nine years. And then...
Who else was in Celestan's band at that time? At that time?
When I first joined Celestan's band, he heard Ernest Kelly playing trombone. Celestan was playing trumpet. A fellow named Abby Foster, not Abby Foster. bamboo
You were talking about Salistan's band, you say Abby Foster, Chinese, was the drummer.
Yes, we had Salistan.
Any other trumpet? He usually used a second trumpet. Do you remember?
Salistan, Guy Kelly, and Ernest Kelly playing trombone.
I never knew Ernest Kelly or anything about him, hardly.

Well, Ernest Kelly peculiarly enough, he was playing a rather modern style of trombone then. Originally, had they split up? They had split. I came after the split. After the split. Yeah. And he had Jeanette Salvant, she was Salvant then, she was playing piano. And Simon Marrera was playing the bass violin. I took John Marrera's place, the banjo player. And Simon Marrera was playing bass violin. And that's about all. The band, Salistan's band, the men changed for quite a few times and around in the beginning of the, in about 29 or 30, we started playing at the Buena Fest and the White House Hotels over in Biloxi.

Oh yes. I have some notes here that Dick Allen, who works with me up at the History Department, he evidently copied this out of a book of some kind. Some personnel, and I thought I might check on that, just to be sure it is accurate. This is the band you were talking about, the Buena Vista and Biloxi. Yeah. He has the date given about 1931.
Adolf Alexander.
With Tats, isn't it? Yeah. Sun Johnson.
Cesar Tonkin.
They might have these, it says the St. Louisianization.
No. No. That, they're trying to get Cecil Thornton. Thornton. Cecil Thornton. Thornton.
That's the name. I'll make a note on here then too.
Yeah.

A lot of people, you know, somebody tells them something and they don't have it on tape, they just make a note and they spell it wrong and can't read their own writing. I'm that way myself. This is said Bill Matthews on trombone. That's in the Biloxi job. Is that right? Yeah.

But this wasn't the first band that we had when we played on that job. We had Oscar Ruzon, I mean Joe Ruzon playing tenor saxophone. And Clarence Hall playing alto saxophone. Bill Matthews playing trombone. Guy Kelly playing trumpet. And Saif Frazier played the drums. Simon Marrera played the bass violin. I played the banjo. And Ricard Alexis played trumpet. Yeah. But this person was Cecil. Not Caesar.
Cecil.
Oh yeah. Cecil.
He was from St. Louis though. Definitely. He's working in the post office in St. Louis. He's a clerk in the post office and he's still playing and he's still arranging. He was a very fine arranger.

Do you remember records that you might have made with him? This Ty Ty Daddy, I remember that, Sweetheart of TKO. That's the recording that I made on there. I was playing banjo on that record. And this note here says that Guy Kelly was trumpet. And Abbey Foster drums had replaced. Yeah, he replaced .
Who had replaced Alexis? Maybe Guy Kelly had replaced Alexis had been there before do you know? at least Alexis had been there before, do you know?
No, Guy Kelly was in the band before Alexis was there.
He was there before.
Yeah, they have this in reverse order. Yeah. Alexis may have replaced Guy Kelly.
I should think so too, as far as Abby Foster would have been there before Sae, certainly, wouldn't he?
Yes, he was there. He was there first.
Did you make any other records? There's one here we've wondered about, this is Jam Up. And when I'm with you.

I don't remember that. I don't remember either of these. I do remember the recording session that we had, but Sweetheart of TKO and Ta Ta Daddy, and we made others. Now, it may have been either of these two. It may have been both of them. I don't know.

We could check from the master number. Usually these numbers here on some of these, this is the serial number. They also have other numbers on there that tell what others were made at the same date. I think we could figure that out. Did you make more than the one date?
You mean the one recording?
Well, the one, did you work with Celestan to make records more than the one time?
No, that was the only time. That was the only time.
In one recording session.

Because during that time, they weren't recording very much, and it was only in recent years that he has made some recording. Within the past seven, eight years that the band, not seven, eight, well, I'll say ten years ago. Ten years, yeah. They made the records then.
Anyway, we can check and find the other titles then.

Speaking about recordings, while I was with Celestan's band, I had composed several numbers, particularly the number, Don't Let Old Age Creep Upon You. And we were in Memphis, Tennessee, and we broadcast from the Peabody Hotel in Memphis. And the numbers were heard by some scouts. They came over to the dance that night, and they asked several times to have it played. So he played it for them. And they came down here, and they wanted to have it recorded. So I told them that since the number originated in Celestan's band, that I felt that I should be loyal to those men to have them recorded. And they didn't want the recording of over six or seven pieces. So in all fairness to the men, I consulted them about it. They told me, they said, well, Kimball, this is your opportunity. And if you get a chance to record your number, you go on. And Joe Robichaux's band, he had a small band then, about seven pieces. And Joan Lunsford was singing with him then. And I had made the arrangement for a seven piece group. And Joe had several other compositions that he wanted to record as well. We went up in the Roosevelt Hotel on the second floor. And it was just a verbal agreement. There wasn't anything written. There wasn't any contract written on it at all. I had it copyrighted, however. And I kept trying to speak with Mr. David Koepp. I told him that I wanted to get an understanding about it. Because I knew that some legal procedure had to be done.
Yeah.

And he didn't ever consider what I was saying. So I had to play that night at the New Orleans Country Club. It was getting late. It was around 6.30 then. I had to be on the job for 8 o'clock. And I told Joe not to record my number. Because I hadn't had any business transactions with Mr. Koepp. So immediately after I left, Mr. Koepp came to Robichaud and said, well, we'll record this. Don't let old age creep upon you. And he said, well, Kimball isn't here now. And he doesn't want it recorded because you all haven't made the proper arrangements or agreements on recording. And he told him that if he didn't record that number, that all the other ones were out. So he recorded it.
It didn't end anyway.

Yeah. And I had attorney Studebaker Lucas. I didn't know that it was published. But I was doing insurance work then. And one of the officials came to me and told me that he had heard a Don't Let Old Age Creep Upon You on a Music Box at Montague's Restaurant on Claiborne Avenue. So I said, I can't believe it. So he said, come on with me and I'll prove it to you. So we went down there.
Was that under that title or had somebody changed the title?
No, it was under that title.
No, it wasn't.
But this is what had been done. It was recorded by the Inc Spots on Decca Record number 1731.
The Caps later organized Decca, you know. Yeah. They started out in Brunswick, I guess. Jack Capp and Dave Capp.
Dave Capp.
Yeah. They still have the Capp records. Jack Capp is dead.
And they asked the proprietor of the place to open the box and to see. by whom the recording was. And my name was on that.
It was on that? Yeah. Did you ever collect royalties for it?

Yes, I collected some royalties. It might have amounted to about maybe seven, eight hundred dollars altogether. But this is what had been done. With the recording that was made by Joe Robichaux's orchestra, the Ink Spots listened to the record, and they sang from that record. But it was not sung in the proper tempo for one thing, and some of the chord changes in the channel, they weren't correct. To me personally, that recording that was made by Robichaux and the one that was made by the Ink Spots wasn't a successful recording. And then with my being displeased as well.
Yeah. If you got on the right breaks, you maybe had a hit on your hand.

But wait, that's not the worst of it. About five years ago, when Deke Watson was down here with the Ink Spots, the groups had changed several times. He told me, in the presence of Walter Pichon, because Walter Pichon introduced me to Deke Watson, he said, there's some of the Ink Spots over there. I said, I don't want to meet them. I said, they're the ones who recorded my number. He said, it isn't their fault. He said, those men were working. Which was true. Yeah, that's right. And he said, come over and meet him. So I went over and talked with him. And Pichon mentioned to him, he said, do you ever remember the number, Don't Let Old Age Creep Up On You? He said, yes. He said, well, that number made ASCAP. He said, it was used in a picture where Cesar Romero and Faye somebody else, I've forgotten who it was, made in 1939 or in 1941. Used it in the movie. He used that picture in the movie. You didn't even know it. I didn't know it. And truthfully, I'm not ashamed to admit it, tears rolled down my face because I knew that I was worth some $50,000 for that.
It should be a good deal. They paid money for that.
And that was something that I lost, regretfully so.
Yeah. Do you know the company? Or I guess too late then to do anything about it? Well, I don't know.
You should have been protected by your copyright. I don't know whether it is still too late. And I may intercede to see whether or not something
can be done. The company is still in business. Must have been one of the major companies.
It must have been.
It changed hands a lot though too, sometimes during the Depression and all that.
But records should be kept of the financing and the remuneration such as it was during
that time. Did you ever renew your copyright? Are you watching that?
No, I haven't renewed it. It's good for 30, 30…

Twenty-six, I think. Twenty-eight years. Twenty-eight? Twenty-eight years and you renew it for another twenty-eight. That's fifty-six. Yeah. Well, it's about time for it to be renewed now. Yeah, the time might be coming up and be worth sharing.

Worthwhile doing. And while I was with Solid Stan's band, I did some of the arranging. We had, when he developed the larger band, we had Cecil Thornton, he was arranging. Fats Pichon did quite a bit of arranging for the band. In fact, Pichon really instructed me. I took a course from Archie Bly, a correspondence course from Archie Bly on arranging. And Fats Pichon coached me along with that. And Cecil Thornton helped me out quite a bit. And I learned to write some.
Well, I wanted to check once more on the Solid Stan band. Did you play banjo or was it bass in the Biloxi?
I played banjo. Banjo. During that time, banjo.
Simon and Marrero were still on bass then? Yes. And when you made the records, were you on bass?
Banjo. Banjo. Banjo.
Oh, I can never remember. Because they have it that way up here, but down here the other one said you were on bass. No, on banjo.
Always banjo.
Yes. Did you ever play on any jobs at all, bass with Celestan in the later years?
Yes, I did. It was by force that I had to do so because my guitar was stolen from me. That same guitar that you see over there.
Oh, yeah.

And the depression had struck rather hard and I wasn't in position then to buy another instrument. And I had my father's instrument, a bass violin. And I said, I had always played on the bass violin. From a child, he stood me on a stool and showed me how the bass was supposed to be fingered.
He wasn't left handed by the way.
No, he was right handed. My mother's left handed. And one of my sisters is left handed. Yeah. My nephew, he's a dentist, he's left handed.
I never noticed. Do you tune your...
It's re-strung. It's strung just the opposite way. You string it up. It's strung for me just as a right hand man would have his strung from him, but it's in the reverse order.
There's a white bass player here, Sherwood Maginapain, pretty good player. You've probably seen him someplace. He plays left handed, but he doesn't bother to re-string his. He plays on...
Just like a right hand man would string his.
He picks up anybody's bass and plays it left handed.

Well, I do that sometimes if I'm out around musicians. You can do it, huh? Really? Yes. If I'm around musicians and they'll ask me to play, I'll first say that, well I can't play because your bass is strung backwards. And then I'll eventually go there. Because I like to play. I like to play both of the instruments.
As long as you don't have to play a whole chord I guess, it's a stick to one string at a time, you can think of a bit more and do it.
But my guitar was stolen from me and during that time the banjos had almost become obsolete around 35. Yes, that's right. And that forced me to play bass violin.
You string your banjo and guitar opposite then too.

Yes. And I started on the bass violin and played that and I continued on playing the bass violin. And I joined Sidney Desvines band again in 1941 and played with him until 47. And that band broke up. Then the Four Tones came in. That was Fred Minor, he was playing guitar in Sidney Desvines band. Louis Barberand was playing drums. And Alvin Alcorn playing trumpet. So we organized a group and called them the Four Tones. We played for two, three years together. And the remaining part of the band was taken over by Joseph Phillips, trumpet player. That group was called Joseph Phillips' Orchestra. And after about two years, William Houston, the pianist in Sidney Desvines band, bought out the ownership from Joe Phillips. And that's William Houston's Orchestra now.
That's after Sidney Desvines already gave up in...
In 47, he gave up in 47.
That was after that.
He left and went to California.
Yes. And we interviewed him out there too. He died, you know, last year.
Yes, he did. And...
I'd never met him. Oh, I'd heard the band years ago here. You might have been with them. About 1942, I guess.
I was playing with him then, playing bass violin. We were playing out the Gypsy Tea Room quite a bit then.
And I heard about, I think, at the San Jacinto Club there.
San Jacinto Club also, yes. We played there quite a bit.
In those days, I didn't know everybody in the band. I didn't know for sure who I heard.

And... After playing with the Four Tones, I began to...we broke up. And I played just as I would be called. Then I later joined Herbert Leary's Orchestra. And I played with him up until now. And about a year and a half ago, I came in charge of the band at the Paddock Lounge. That's how I got to Dixieland Group. And I played with Albert French's office. He has a tuxedo band. I played with him on the out-of-town engagements because his bass players sometimes can't get away from work.
Yes, he told me that. And I'm hoping I'd catch you sometime with him, but I didn't... Yes. And now you have your own group down there on St. Peter's Street at Haysha. So, this is really a nice group.

Thank you very much. I would like to see that group develop because... I feel that the Dixieland music has great potential now. There was such a change in the trend of music when rock and roll came in. I'm not speaking against rock and roll because... It fills the place. It has a good picture. It has its merit. It definitely has its merit. But, it had gone so far away from the real music until something had to come back and bring it back to its normalcy. And I think that Dixieland is about the only thing that can do it. That's why I would like, if such as possible, to have my group develop. We are playing down there, as you know, on the 7th again.
Oh, on the 7th of December.
Yeah, on December. And I hope that you'll be there to hear it.
There's one other thing that Dick Allen had here on a note. Something about when we interviewed Charlie Love, we interviewed him a couple of times.
I played with Charlie Love too. Yeah, he made it.
I'm going to draw this door. Pardon me just a minute, Eddie. I'll be with you in a little while.
We'll be through here. We can quit at any time.
Alright. We don't have to finish up this.
There was a band. Listen to this. I want that to go on record. Talking about being in a theater.
In a theater? Yeah. Maybe he heard you with Jeanette once. She played piano with you in the theater.
Well, she was my first wife. Yes, I knew that.
Yeah.
In a theater now. I can't remember.
Maybe he played with you in the theater. I don't know. He used to do a lot of show work too.

No, when Jeanette first started, she used to play in the theater over in Gulfport. She was the one who played in the theater. We haven't interviewed her, but the right reason we will. When she was a girl, that's where she started. Her father used to take her from Pascos down down to Gulfport and he would...
We can get that part of the story then from her. Yes. You were going to tell about this story about...

One little group that I played with, I can't remember whether it was before I started playing with Paul Mollier, whether it was shortly afterwards, before I had gone to St. Louis, but there was Mr. Mineta, a fellow named Red Dugas playing drums. Oh yeah. A trombone player, his name was Freddie Babu.
Yeah, maybe heard the name, but I don't know anything about him. Freddie Babu. Yeah. I played some bandages, somebody might have mentioned that.
And Joe Robichaux and I, I was playing banjo then. And we played at a little place down on Charter Street. It was only for a short while. We played there on...
Well, where on Charter? There's nothing here.
Either Charter or Decatur, but it was down there about Toulouse, somewhere in that area down there. It was frequented by seamen.
Yeah, probably maybe Decatur then. Most likely. Several people told us they played there.

Oh yeah, and this is something else that I'd like to go in the interview. I feel that I owe this to a friend of mine, because we started out as musicians together. And to be perfectly frank, the first organized group that I played in was in the high school orchestra. And Professor Valmo Victor, he's a retired school teacher now. He's still around now. He's still here in New Orleans. And it would be nice if you wouldn't interview him. Yeah, it would be nice if I could interview him. What is the whole name again now?
Valmo Victor.
Valmo Victor.
Do you know?
He's a pianist.
Would he be in the phone book?

I'm sure that he is. I'm sure that he is. He's responsible for many musicians, many good musicians. Lord Jack Willis that plays trumpet, he taught him to play music. Al Goodman, the bass player, you've heard of him? Heard of him, yeah. He's a very fine bass player. Another fellow that they called Foots is a drummer.
Oh yeah, I heard of him.

He was in that group. And many of the musicians who were playing with some big bands away from here now, they started under him as a teacher. Valmo and I were classmates. And he played the piano for the groups to sing. A boy named Hannibal played the violin. The two grand brothers, one played violin and the other played clarinet. And we had a little group that would play for little afternoon class parties. And I had my banjo. And we thought that we were something with that group that we had. But I always said that in the event that I should ever be interviewed, I would always feel as though I should pay a tribute to Valmo Victor because he definitely is a fine musician. And he plays all instruments. He taught all instruments.
He taught the music then in the schools too?

No, he didn't teach. We were schoolmates together. Then he was a school teacher. And then he had. He taught other subjects. Yeah, he taught literary subjects. But he had at his home, he taught many private lessons. And he had quite a few students that he thought were successful. So that's, I feel satisfied now that I've paid that tribute to him.

Yeah, well, that's a part of them because a lot of those men we never hear of, you know. Unless they've been in the public eye at present or late years, we wouldn't hear of them. There's one other thing I was going to ask just for a minute, if you have a minute to think of any other banjo players or bass players that might have influenced you even if you didn't study with them or maybe you got ideas or that you admired when you were younger.
Well, this will take me back to school again. There was a place that's the Louisiana Bank at Gravia and, no, it's not Gravia now, but it's in that commercial area down there.
Yeah, that's that.
The Louisiana Bank, well that was the Pythian Temple at one time. Oh, sure. They had a roof garden there.
Yeah.
And we would have our school dances on the roof garden. It was a very lovely place. And in Manuel Perez's band, there was a banjo player named Caffrey.
Oh, yes.
He's dead now. He's from . Caffrey Dierensburg.
That's right, Caffrey Dierensburg. I don't know about him, yeah.
He was from Texas. He lived in Texas in the later years. George Gaino says he was great.
He was.

He was. A couple of others. George Gaino plays very, very, pardon me, he plays very, very similar to the style that Caffrey played, the picking style. Yeah. And there was a number that we all loved to hear him play, was sitting in a corner. And he used to pick that beautifully. Now, he was what I might say, interested me in playing music, because when I would go to the dances, there's very little dancing I would do, I would listen to his playing. Now, as a bass player, as I said before, I played bass by a matter of force, because I couldn't afford to buy another guitar after that one was stolen from me. Probably. And I took up my father's instrument, and after having practiced on it for five or six months, I just felt as though I was able to come out and play. So I did. Not that I was playing as I should have been playing, but it's supplemented anyway. It shouldn't have been too difficult after your bands are working. No.
And then— Excuse me if you interrupt, I think I'd better ask. In regard to the old times when they played string bass, I've heard they used the bow more. Do you remember your father? Did he—
I had my father's bow. I had my father's bow in this house right here someplace now.
Did he bow as much as he picked in the—
He bowed more.
With more.
And—
Even with Fate's band, like when you were working with him, did he bow at the

deal in those days too? He bowed. He did. Because it has been mentioned, if you talk with Willie Umfrey, he will tell you that my daddy had a stroke with the bow that was similar to one using the Pizzicotta. When he would pull the bow, he would pull it with force, you know. Yeah. And give it a lift. Yeah. That's why he was appreciated as a bass player. Most of his playing was done with the bow.
With the bow, right? I'd heard that the old timers did that. I wonder about your father, I suppose. Yeah.
Yes, he played with the bow.
Is there anything else you want to add about your father or your life? I don't want to keep you all after me.
Well, no. I feel honored, as I told you before, to be interviewed. I hope that that that I have given you will be of some worth.

It certainly is, because you're one of the famous bass and banjo players, especially, we've always heard about you and your father, of course, is one of the real pioneers. So, it's really an honor for us to be able to talk to such a musical family and hear directly. Thank you very much. I'm surprised to hear about your father's brothers. They sang and Andrew was his brother then. You don't know anything about what happened to him or was he older than your father? No, he was younger than my father.

He was younger than my father. He was younger. There was a family mix up there. They didn't ever get along too well because, well, that was some of the old seeds that were sold by my grandfather. Yeah, occasionally. I mean, that's an art in the family.
Things happen like that.

In families that they don't. But I sure mentioned when I came home after having learned, because we went into detail about it and as to just what it was, and I mentioned to my father exactly what it was. He said that he had always intended to tell me and that now that I was a man that he felt free to tell me that. But being my father and of the immediate family that we had, he didn't want anything to come home or, you know, I said, but things will out.
Yeah, well, I certainly appreciate all of the information that you've told us.
Well, I've done the best that I could.

That certainly was, and I certainly enjoyed hearing you. I never really got to hear you. I heard you years ago when I didn't even know who you were, like with Desvene. I look forward to hearing your band again. Well, thank you very much.

segments.title: Opening and Kimball's name
segments.summary: Recording notes, date of 25 Nov 1961, and why Kimball was called Henry Kimball Jr. though his name is Narvin.

segments.title: Birth and boyhood in the Irish Channel
segments.summary: Born March 1909 near 7th and St. Thomas; Irish and Black neighbours looked after each other's children yet boys fought across ward lines.

segments.title: Wagon bands and lawn parties
segments.summary: Advertising wagons with tailgate trombone and bass at the back, two bands playing against each other.

segments.chapter: Henry Kimball and the Kimball family
segments.title: Father Henry Kimball's birth and death
segments.summary: His father's approximate birth year, that he played bass violin and later sousaphone, and died at about 53 in 1932-33.

segments.chapter: Henry Kimball and the Kimball family
segments.title: Father's training and early instruments
segments.summary: Father played with Robichaux, studied with Professor Nicholson, started on small violin in a school band, then bass violin.

segments.chapter: Henry Kimball and the Kimball family
segments.title: Southern University and Kimball's own schools
segments.summary: Discussion of the Southern University and New Orleans University schools; Kimball's own schooling at James Lewis, McDonogh 35 and New Orleans University.

segments.chapter: Henry Kimball and the Kimball family
segments.title: Father with John Robichaux's orchestra
segments.summary: Robichaux's was his father's first organized band; Kimball heard it at the Lyric Theater around age eight or nine and names the lineup.

segments.chapter: Henry Kimball and the Kimball family
segments.title: Andrew Kimball and the Kimball brothers
segments.summary: Discovering that trumpeter Andrew Kimball was his father's brother, and the singing quartet of brothers.

segments.title: First instruments: piano, violin and a homemade banjo
segments.summary: He disliked piano and violin, built a stringed instrument from a seagull box, and Coochie Martin's guitar strings; the kitchen trio.

segments.title: Onfrey and Duran band and Maurice Duran
segments.summary: Russell asks about bands of Coochie Martin's era; Kimball recalls Onfrey and Duran; news of Maurice Duran's death.

segments.title: Ukulele in high school
segments.summary: Buying a ukulele with savings, admiring Red Allen's playing, and linking dates to his father's start on the Capitol.

segments.title: Father on the steamer Capitol with Armstrong
segments.summary: Father played the Capitol with Armstrong, St. Cyr and Baby Dodds and roomed with Louis on the boat.

segments.title: Banjo lessons and joining Fate Marable's band on the Capitol
segments.summary: Father bought him a banjo and Willie Foster taught him; then called to rehearse in St. Louis, arranging exams, and struggling to read the banjo book.

segments.title: Marable band personnel
segments.summary: Kimball lists the men on the boat band: Campbell, Marable, Humphrey, Story, Dewey Jackson, Irvin Randolph.

segments.title: Replaced after Charlie Creff arrives
segments.summary: Charlie Creff wanted Al Morgan and Red Brown back, so Kimball and his father got notice; Kimball's illness.

segments.title: Paul Mollier's family band
segments.summary: The Mollier family band on Dumaine Street, its members, and old trombonist Joe Petit.

segments.title: Joe Petit's trombone and leaving Mollier for the boat
segments.summary: Russell's recording of Petit with Wooden Joe, his one-tooth embouchure, and Mollier's blessing for the boat job.

segments.title: Sidney Desvignes band
segments.summary: Three months with Desvignes after the boat; the rhythm and sax sections; Russell's meeting with a train cook.

segments.title: Joining Celestin's band
segments.summary: Contest nights at the Bulls Club, then eight or nine years with Celestin; personnel and the split band.

segments.title: Biloxi job and band personnel check
segments.summary: Checking a note about the Buena Vista and White House hotels in Biloxi and Celestin recording personnel.

segments.title: Celestin recording session
segments.summary: He recalls only one recording session with Celestin, and cannot identify some titles.

segments.title: Don't Let Old Age Creep Upon You: the Robichaux recording
segments.summary: His song was recorded by Joe Robichaux without agreement, then by the Ink Spots; he got a few royalties.

segments.title: Learning of the film use and lost royalties
segments.summary: Deke Watson says the song was in a film; Kimball weeps at lost money and talks about copyright renewal.

segments.title: Learning to arrange
segments.summary: Arranging for Celestin's larger band with help from Cecil Thornton, Fats Pichon and a correspondence course.

segments.title: Banjo or bass in Celestin's band
segments.summary: Russell checks whether Kimball played banjo or bass on the Biloxi job and records.

segments.title: Switching to bass violin and playing left-handed
segments.summary: His guitar was stolen during the Depression so he used his father's bass; he restrings it left-handed.

segments.title: Desvignes again, the Four Tones and William Houston
segments.summary: Rejoining Desvignes 1941-47, forming the Four Tones, and the band's becoming Houston's Orchestra.

segments.title: Recent work and hopes for Dixieland
segments.summary: Herbert Leary, Albert French, leading the band at the Paddock Lounge, and his view of Dixieland versus rock and roll.

segments.title: Charlie Love and Jeanette's theater playing
segments.summary: Brief mention of Charlie Love, and Jeanette, his first wife, who played piano in a Gulfport theater.

segments.title: Small group with Robichaux on Decatur Street
segments.summary: A short stint with Mineta, Red Dugas and Freddie Babu in a seamen's place near Toulouse.

segments.title: Tribute to Professor Valmo Victor
segments.summary: Kimball's schoolmate and teacher Valmo Victor, who taught many New Orleans musicians.

segments.title: Caffrey Dierensburg and bass by necessity
segments.summary: Banjoist Caffrey with Manuel Perez inspired him; school dances at the Pythian roof garden.

segments.title: Father's bowing style
segments.summary: His father bowed more than he plucked, and Willie Humphrey praised his stroke.

segments.title: Closing questions on the Kimball family rift
segments.summary: Thanks and a note on the family's quarrel over his grandfather, which his father explained.

segments.title: Goodbyes
segments.summary: Thanks and closing remarks.
